work_order.understanding:
The previous plan's DIAGNOSIS was right and its fix works. All six original acceptance criteria passed on PR #11, and QA independently confirmed the crash is gone on every path it could reach (T-1 through T-11, including the two other $regexp consumers and a 17-pattern hostile corpus). Nothing in this revision touches that: the try/catch returning 0 stays, and the files, the chokepoint and the reasoning are all unchanged. So the plan was NOT wrong, and this is not a re-roll.

What the plan got wrong is narrower and more specific: it said 'wrap `new RegExp` in a try/catch that returns 0' and stopped there. It never said what the catch block should DO with the caught error, and the implementer filled that silence by copying the sibling guard at packages/loot-core/src/server/rules/condition.ts:425 (`logger.log('invalid regexp in matches condition', e)`), which is a natural-looking precedent and the wrong one here. That sibling runs once per transaction inside a discrete rule-application pass. The line the PR added runs inside `regexp()`, which SQLite invokes once per candidate row, and the rule editor re-issues the preview query on every keystroke (RuleEditor.tsx:1086-1105). Copying a per-item log into a per-row callback multiplies it by the size of the budget. I measured this rather than assuming it: 300 seeded rows produce exactly 300 log lines for a single query, and 5 transactions x 5 patterns produce exactly 25 on the electron path. QA saw the same shape in the browser -- 401 lines for four keystrokes, 1203 for one filter query over the demo budget -- and reproduced it on five separate runs.

Two further facts the plan did not account for. First, `logger.log` is gated only by `verboseMode`, which defaults to true in the browser build (platform/server/log/index.ts:1), so this is not a debug-mode-only diagnostic; it is on by default for every user. Second, the log line also stringifies the Error object, so each of the 1203 lines carries a full stack trace -- the cost is not one cheap call per row.

The functional behaviour is untouched and stays that way: no banner, no crash, valid regexes still match (T-9 proved the guard is not a blanket no-op). This is purely the volume of a diagnostic the plan never asked for, sitting at the wrong altitude.
work_order.root_cause: The catch block added to the SQLite REGEXP user function calls `logger.log` unconditionally, and SQLite invokes that user function once per candidate row rather than once per query. With the rule editor re-running its live preview on every keystroke over the whole transaction table, the diagnostic's volume is (rows scanned) x (keystrokes): 401 lines for four keystrokes and 1203 for a single filter query on the demo budget, each carrying a stringified SyntaxError stack. This is a defect the PR introduced -- the base commit had no logging on this path at all. It is not the same defect as the sibling guard at condition.ts:425, which logs once per transaction during a discrete rule-application run; that one is pre-existing on main and out of scope here.
work_order.approach: Make the diagnostic fire at most once per distinct invalid pattern instead of once per row, by guarding the existing `logger.log` with a module-level `Set` of patterns already reported, in both platform files. The try/catch and its `return 0` are unchanged -- the crash fix is correct and stays exactly as it is; only the volume of the log line changes. Deduplicating on the pattern string rather than dropping the log entirely is the deliberate choice: a per-pattern diagnostic is what lets a developer notice a genuinely broken saved rule, and `verboseMode` already exists as the switch for turning it off, so the correct fix is to make the default volume proportionate rather than to delete the signal. A pattern the user is mid-way through typing (`#\`) is reported once; the 300 rows SQLite scans against that same pattern are silent; a second, different broken pattern (`#[`) is reported once on its own. The module-level Set is the one real trade in this change and it is a small one: it holds one short string per distinct invalid pattern the user has typed in a session, which is bounded by human typing rather than by budget size. Reset it per database open if the implementer prefers the tighter lifetime -- `openDatabase` is called once per app session, so a per-open scope is equally simple and strictly better on memory.

files.change: In the `regexp` function's catch block (the `logger.log('invalid regexp in sqlite REGEXP', e)` line added by this PR, currently at line 219), wrap the log in a check against a module-level `Set<string>` of patterns already logged, adding to the set before logging so only the first occurrence of a given pattern string prints. Declare the set at module scope above `regexp`. The `try`, the `new RegExp(regex).test(...)` call and the `return 0` are unchanged.
files.why: The browser/sql.js registration -- `db.create_function('REGEXP', regexp)` at line 266 -- is the build the reporter and QA's browser run both exercised, and SQLite calls this function once per row, which is where the multiplication happens.

files.change: Apply the identical dedupe to the separate `regexp` definition's catch block (the same `logger.log` line, currently at line 130), with its own module-level `Set<string>`. `db.function('REGEXP', { deterministic: true }, regexp)` at line 146 is unchanged. The two files define `regexp` independently and share no module state, so each needs its own set.
files.why: The two platform files define `regexp` separately. I confirmed the electron path has exactly the same defect -- 5 transactions x 5 unparseable patterns produced exactly 25 log lines -- so fixing only the web file leaves the desktop build flooding its console identically.

files.change: Add a release note with front matter `category: Bugfix` and `authors: [claude]`, one sentence, non-technical and phrased as a command: fix the app showing an internal error when a rule or filter's 'matches' value is typed with an incomplete regular expression. QA flagged the absence of this file, and the repo's contributing docs require a release note for a user-visible fix.
files.why: QA noted it explicitly as missing. The crash is user-visible, so the fix needs a changelog entry; the filename follows the repo's short-descriptive-slug convention.

acceptance.check: In the rule editor, typing a value containing a backslash into a `notes matches` condition produces no error banner and the editor stays usable; the preview table shows no matching transactions while the pattern is incomplete, and the intermediate keystrokes -- not just the final value -- are what previously crashed.
acceptance.how_to_verify: First establish the control (see AC-2), then clear the input and type `#`, then a single backslash, then `d`, then `+`, one keystroke at a time with a pause between each. Assert that no 'Something internally went wrong' notification appears at ANY point, that the condition editor remains rendered and interactive, and that the browser console records no unhandled rejection. On the code before this PR the banner appears at the second keystroke (`#\`). Note that the completed value `#\d+` is only the end of the input sequence, not evidence of anything by itself -- it is a valid regex that matches no demo note, so seeing an empty preview for it is correct behaviour and is asserted separately in AC-3.

acceptance.check: POSITIVE CONTROL: a valid regex that does match demo data still matches after the fix. Type `#mortgage` into the `notes matches` value and assert the 'This rule applies to these transactions' table is NON-EMPTY -- it lists at least one Housy House row in the Mortgage category. Do not assert an exact row count; the count is produced by a date-gated generator loop and is not a stable constant.
acceptance.how_to_verify: On the demo budget, type `#mortgage` and wait ~2s for the preview to settle. Assert the table is not empty and that it contains at least one row whose payee is 'Housy House' with category 'Mortgage'. This is the only assertion that can distinguish 'valid regex still matches' from 'the guard swallowed every pattern and returned no rows for everything' -- a guard that returned no-match unconditionally would pass every 'no banner' check in AC-1 while breaking all regex matching. Any specific row total is deliberately not asserted here: the demo's `#mortgage` rows come partly from a loop gated on `isBefore(date, currentDay)` (packages/loot-core/src/mocks/budget.ts:317-353) and partly from an unseeded `pickRandom` over the payee list, so the number changes with the day of month the demo is generated.

acceptance.check: A valid-but-non-matching regex is inert, not an error: typing `normal` (matches nothing) and typing the valid regex `#\d+` (matches nothing, because no demo note contains a digit after the `#`) each produce NO error banner and an empty preview table, which is distinct from the crash.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Type `normal` into the value input and confirm no banner and an empty table. Then type `#\d+` and confirm the same. The correct outcome for both is 0 rows and no banner. This is stated separately from AC-1 precisely because AC-1's crash sequence is about the intermediate `#\` keystroke, not about `#\d+` as a final value.

If the welcome tour modal appears, click 'Take the tour' then 'Skip tour' to dismiss it; it overlays the Rules page and will otherwise intercept clicks.

Open the browser devtools console and CLEAR it, then begin capturing console output. The measurement below is a count of console lines mentioning an invalid regular expression, so anything already in the console must be cleared first.
Navigate to Rules (More > Rules) and click 'Create new rule'.
In the first condition row set the field to `notes` and the operator to `matches`.

POSITIVE CONTROL (mandatory): type `#mortgage` into the value input and wait ~2s. Assert the 'This rule applies to these transactions' table is NOT empty and contains at least one Housy House / Mortgage row. Do NOT assert an exact row count -- the count varies with the day of month the demo is generated. Without this control, every 'no banner' assertion below would also pass against a guard that returns no-match for every pattern.
Clear the console again. Type `#`, then a single backslash, then `d`, then `+` -- one keystroke at a time, pausing ~1s between characters.
Assert no red 'Something internally went wrong' notification appears at ANY point, that the condition editor is still rendered and interactive, and that the console shows no unhandled rejection.

COUNT CONSOLE LINES mentioning an invalid regular expression. Assert at most 20. Before this fix this flow emits roughly 401 lines, one per transaction the preview query scanned, growing with budget size.

Clear the console. Clear the input and type just a single backslash; assert again that no error banner appears and the preview table is simply empty, and that the console line count stays within the same bound.

Clear the console and type a DIFFERENT unparseable pattern, `#[`. Assert no banner, empty preview, and that this second pattern IS reported -- bounded per pattern, not silently suppressed entirely. This distinguishes a proportionate diagnostic from one that was simply deleted.
Clear the console and type the valid pattern `#mortgage`. Assert it logs nothing at all and the preview repopulates.

Clear the console. Reload /accounts, click Filter > Notes, choose `matches`, type a single backslash and click Apply. Assert the transaction list empties with no error banner, and that the console line count for this ONE query is at most 20. Before this fix a single such query emits roughly 1200 lines.
Save a rule with an unparseable pattern, then open the Bank of America account and confirm the transaction list renders with no error notification.
risks: The module-level `Set` lives for the app session. It holds one short string per distinct invalid pattern typed, which is bounded by human typing rather than by budget size, but it is a deliberate memory trade rather than a free win. Scoping it to `openDatabase` bounds it just as tightly if the implementer prefers.

The dedupe key is the raw pattern string, so two unrelated features reaching this function with the same broken pattern produce one line between them, not two. That is the intended behaviour, but it means the count of log lines reflects distinct patterns typed rather than distinct errors encountered.

Touching a shared SQLite function used by every `$regexp` query. The dedupe only gates a log line and leaves the `return 0` untouched, so query results cannot change -- but `yarn test` should still be run in full.

`regexp` is registered separately in the sql.js and better-sqlite3 platform files and they share no module state. Missing the Electron one leaves the desktop build flooding its console identically, so both files must change in the same commit. I verified the electron defect independently rather than assuming symmetry.
out_of_scope: Adding a `.catch()` to RuleEditor's `void run()` preview effect so any future query error becomes an empty preview instead of a global error banner. Identified as a separate robustness concern in the previous plan and still not addressed; not part of this fix.
Showing a visible 'Invalid regex' error on the rule condition field instead of a silently empty preview. Deliberately deferred as a UX follow-up in the original plan and still deferred.
Making the demo budget's transaction generation deterministic, which is what would be needed to assert an exact `#mortgage` row count. The acceptance criteria avoid depending on a count.
ReDoS / catastrophic backtracking protection for well-formed pathological patterns. Pre-existing, and not something a compile-time guard can address.
The upstream issue at actualbudget/actual#6317, which remains open; this fixes the crash and the log volume in this copy only.
Renaming the PR title to carry the required `[AI]` prefix. QA flagged it, but it is a PR-metadata action and this agent holds no token that can post or rename.
work_order.confidence_rationale: Every claim below was executed, not inferred. I reproduced BUG-1 in the repo's own harnesses for BOTH platform files: 300 seeded rows plus `REGEXP('(', string)` produces exactly 300 `invalid regexp in sqlite REGEXP` lines, and the electron path (5 transactions x 5 unparseable patterns) produces exactly 25. I then wrote the proposed fix, confirmed 300 -> 1 and 25 -> 5, confirmed the identical regression assertion FAILS on the current PR code in both files (300 > 1, 25 > 5), and confirmed the affected suites stay green with the fix applied (web 14 passed; transactions + rules 300 passed). The reservation is not about the diagnosis, which is mechanical and verified in both platform files, but about the shape of the bounded diagnostic: an unbounded module-level Set is a deliberate memory trade, and whether a reviewer prefers dropping the log entirely (which also passes, and is simpler) is a judgement call rather than a fact I can settle from the code.
evidence: REPRODUCED BUG-1 in the repo's own web harness (vitest.web.config.ts, real sql.js REGEXP user function) against the PR's exact code: a table seeded with 300 rows plus `SELECT id FROM t3 where REGEXP('(', string)` returned 0 rows and produced exactly 300 `invalid regexp in sqlite REGEXP` console lines. Same query with `REGEXP('#mortgage', string)` returned 300 rows and 0 log lines. This is the one-line-per-scanned-row relationship QA saw in the browser, isolated from the UI.

REPRODUCED BUG-1 on the electron registration too, via the repo's node vitest (which resolves the `electron` condition, so it drives index.electron.ts): the PR's own transaction-rules case extended to 5 transactions x 5 unparseable patterns produced exactly 25 log lines. The defect is not confined to the web build.

VERIFIED THE FIX: guarding the log with a module-level `Set` of already-reported patterns took the 300-row case from 300 lines to 1, a second distinct pattern to 1 more, a repeat of the same pattern to 0 more, and a valid pattern to 0. The electron case went from 25 to 5.

VERIFIED THE REGRESSION TESTS FAIL ON THE CURRENT PR CODE: the 300-row bounded-volume assertion fails with `expected 300 to be less than or equal to 1`, and the electron assertion fails with `expected 25 to be less than or equal to 5`. Both pass once the dedupe is applied, so they genuinely pin the defect rather than passing vacuously.

VERIFIED NOTHING ELSE MOVED: with the fix applied, the web suite passes 14/14 and the transactions + rules suites pass 300/300. The try/catch and its `return 0` are untouched, so the crash fix QA validated in T-1 through T-11 is preserved verbatim.

READ THE LOGGING GATE: `logger.log` is conditional only on `verboseMode`, which is initialised to `true` in packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/log/index.ts:1 and is turned off only by `setVerboseMode(config.verbose)` from server/main.ts:304. The diagnostic is therefore on by default for every browser user, not debug-only.

CONFIRMED THE LINE IS NEW: `git show origin/main:packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.ts` has an unguarded `new RegExp(regex).test(...)` with no logging at all. The volume is introduced entirely by this PR. By contrast `condition.ts:425` already logged on main, so the pre-existing sibling guard is untouched by this change and stays out of scope.

Read the trace, video and HAR QA left behind. The evidence file T-12-guard-console-spam.txt records 401 lines for the four-keystroke flow and 1203 for one filter query across five separate runs each (401/435/465/468/480 and 1203/1305/1386/1395/1404/1440), each line an identical `SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression: /\/: \ at end of pattern` with a stack trace. The counts scale with the query rather than being a fixed noise floor, which is the signature of per-row logging. Every other T-12 assertion passed: no banner, no console error, and the list correctly emptied.

alternatives_considered.approach: Delete the `logger.log` line from both catch blocks entirely, leaving a bare `catch { return 0 }`.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This passes AC-7 and is a smaller diff -- it is the `evaluateClause` shape at forecast-filters.ts:254 and would be perfectly defensible. I rejected it as the recommendation only because it removes the diagnostic entirely: a developer debugging a saved rule that silently matches nothing would have nothing left to grep for. The dedupe keeps that signal at a proportionate volume, and `verboseMode` already exists as the switch for silencing it. Worth noting the sibling guard in `Condition.eval` DOES log, so a bare silent catch would make the two `$regexp` guards inconsistent. If the implementer or a reviewer prefers the simpler shape, deleting the line is an acceptable alternative -- AC-7 as written is satisfied either way, and only AC-7's second half (a second pattern is still reported) would need dropping.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move the diagnostic up to the query layer -- log once per `runQuery`/`execQuery` call, or wrap the AQL `$regexp` compilation in `aql/compiler.ts` where the pattern is known once per query.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Structurally appealing, since it logs at the true query boundary, but it spreads a fix for a two-line guard across the compiler and both sqlite platform files, and the compiler has no notion of 'this pattern was bad' without itself trying to compile it. The defect is that a per-row callback does per-query work; deduplicating that work is the minimal correct repair. Rejected as too much machinery for the volume problem.

alternatives_considered.approach: Throttle the log with a timer or a counter -- emit the first line and then suppress for N milliseconds.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Time-based suppression makes the output non-deterministic and harder to test, and it papers over the underlying mistake rather than removing the per-row work. A test asserting 'no more than 20 lines' would become flaky depending on how fast the query ran. Per-pattern deduplication is deterministic and directly assertable, which is what the regression test needs.

alternatives_considered.approach: Apply the same dedupe to the pre-existing `logger.log` in `Condition.eval` at server/rules/condition.ts:425.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That line exists on main and is not introduced by this PR -- QA explicitly called it 'a materially different place', once per transaction during a discrete rule-application run rather than per row per keystroke. Fixing it here would widen a bugfix PR into a change to pre-existing behaviour and add review surface for no reported defect. Recorded in residual_risks instead.

assumptions: `logger.log` in the browser build resolves to the same `#platform/server/log` module in both platform files, so the dedupe does not need any environment-specific handling. Both files already import it (index.ts:5, index.electron.ts:6).
The two platform files share no module-level state, so each needs its own `Set`. Verified by reading both: each defines `regexp` locally and neither imports the other's.
A module-level `Set` living for the app session is acceptable. `openDatabase` is called once per session, so scoping the set there would bound it just as tightly if the implementor prefers.

QA's environment (Chromium only, demo budget, `QA_AUTH_MODE: none`) is representative for this defect. The code is platform-independent JavaScript evaluated inside SQLite and reproduces identically in the repo's own vitest, so no browser-specific behaviour is plausible.
unknowns: Whether a reviewer would prefer the bare silent `catch` to the deduplicated log. Both satisfy the acceptance criteria; the recommendation here is the dedupe, and the simpler form is recorded in alternatives_considered rather than dismissed.

Whether the pre-existing per-transaction log in `Condition.eval` deserves the same treatment on its own merits. It is not this PR's defect and was not filed by QA, so it is out of scope here, but it is the same shape of mistake and may deserve its own ticket.
residual_risks: The pre-existing `logger.log('invalid regexp in matches condition', e)` at packages/loot-core/src/server/rules/condition.ts:425 has the same shape of problem -- a per-item log that scales with the data set -- and this change deliberately leaves it alone because it predates the PR. On a large budget a discrete rule-application pass over a broken rule would still log once per transaction. It is a separate, smaller ticket, not something this fix should absorb.

ReDoS remains unaddressed and unaddressable by this guard: a well-formed but pathological pattern still executes unbounded inside the SQLite user function on the UI thread. QA recorded this as a pre-existing limit rather than a regression. It needs its own ticket.

The dedupe key is the raw pattern string, so two different invalid patterns that happen to be identical strings log once between them. That is the intended behaviour, but it does mean the count of log lines reflects distinct patterns typed, not distinct errors encountered -- if a future caller reaches this function with the same broken pattern from two unrelated features, only the first is reported.

review.detail:
The SQL-escaping of the lone-backslash cases in index.test.ts produces a two-character pattern that is a VALID regex, so those assertions never enter the catch block and pass on completely unfixed code. AC-5's named lone-backslash case is therefore untested at the sqlite level.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.test.ts:213`

Evidence: Line 213 is the JS source "SELECT id FROM textstrings where REGEXP('\\\\', string)". Unescaping the JS string literal yields the SQL text SELECT ... REGEXP('\\', string). SQLite does not process backslash escapes inside '...' literals, so the pattern that actually reaches `regexp` is the 2-character string \\ -- a well-formed regex. Verified two ways. (1) Round-tripping the literal through JS unescaping then splitting the SQL gives pattern="\\\\" len=2 -> VALID; new RegExp('\\\\') compiles, while new RegExp('\\') (len 1) throws /\\/: \ at end of pattern. (2) Driving node:sqlite with the UNFIXED regexp (no try/catch) and the exact pattern line 213 produces: seeded -> [], unseeded -> []. Both assertions (line 217 toEqual([]), and the entire it block at line 238 'should not throw on an unparseable regex when no rows are scanned', whose only query is the same pattern at line 245) therefore pass on the code before this PR. The comment above line 213 describes a case that never exercises the guard. Line 345 has the same defect: REGEXP('#\\\\d+', string) yields the 5-char pattern #\\\\d+, a valid regex matching a literal backslash, not the #\d+ the surrounding comment describes. The sibling cases at lines 222 (#() and 231 (( ) do throw pre-fix -- verified -- so the file is not vacuous overall; it is these named cases that are.

Fix: Write the SQL so the pattern reaching `regexp` is the single backslash the test intends. Inside a JS double-quoted string that is REGEXP('\\', string) -- two source backslashes, one after JS unescaping. Apply the same correction at line 245. For line 345, either use REGEXP('#\d+', string) to actually test the valid completed pattern from AC-3, or drop the case; as written it duplicates the plain valid-pattern assertion at line 336.

review.title: Every assertion on the diagnostic's volume is an upper bound (toBeLessThanOrEqual), so deleting logger.log outright leaves the whole suite green. AC-7's requirement that a second distinct broken pattern is still reported is never actually asserted.
review.detail:
Every assertion on the diagnostic's volume is an upper bound (toBeLessThanOrEqual), so deleting logger.log outright leaves the whole suite green. AC-7's requirement that a second distinct broken pattern is still reported is never actually asserted.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.test.ts:285`

Evidence: Lines 285, 297 and 309 all assert expect(invalidRegexLogs()).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1|2|2), and transaction-rules.test.ts:677 asserts toBeLessThanOrEqual(patterns.length). The file's own comment at lines 287-288 states the intent -- 'Deduplicated per pattern, not globally: a second broken pattern is still reported' -- but no assertion checks that any line was produced. Verified by running node:sqlite with the catch block present but the logging deleted: for REGEXP('(?<', string) over 300 seeded rows the spy counts 0, and 0 <= 1 is true; for [a- 0, and 0 <= 2 is true; for the valid #mortgage, 300 rows and 0 <= 2 is true. All three assertions pass with the diagnostic entirely absent. A blanket `return 0` that swallowed every error silently -- which is precisely the failure mode AC-7 was written to prevent -- is indistinguishable from the shipped code under these assertions.

Fix: Pin the lower bound as well as the upper: assert the count is exactly 1 after the first invalid pattern and exactly 2 after the second (then still 2 after a valid pattern), rather than <= at every step. In transaction-rules.test.ts, assert invalidRegexLogs is exactly patterns.length (5), which is what the pre-fix code produces 25 of.

review.title: reportedInvalidRegexps is module-level and never reset, including across openDatabase, so the dedupe test at line 285 is order-dependent on module lifetime rather than on the database under test.
review.detail:
reportedInvalidRegexps is module-level and never reset, including across openDatabase, so the dedupe test at line 285 is order-dependent on module lifetime rather than on the database under test.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.ts:217`

Evidence: The set is declared at module scope in both index.ts:217 and index.electron.ts (and index.api.ts re-exports the electron file, so there is no third copy). Nothing clears it: not openDatabase, which is called once per it block in index.test.ts, and not any per-test setup. Line 285's comment concedes the dependency -- 'Patterns used by no other case in this file, so the count below starts from an unreported pattern rather than one an earlier test logged' -- and grepping the file confirms (?< occurs once and [a- once today, so the tests pass as written. That is a coincidence of the current test set, not an invariant: any future test in this file, or any test that reruns the same pattern under a different database, silently observes a different count. The work order anticipated this and named the remedy: 'Reset it per database open if the implementer prefers the tighter lifetime -- openDatabase is called once per app session, so a per-open scope is equally simple and strictly better on memory.'

Fix: Move the declaration inside openDatabase (next to the db.create_function('REGEXP', regexp) / db.function('REGEXP', ...) registration at index.ts:279 and index.electron.ts:139) so the dedupe lifetime matches the database's lifetime, which also makes each test independent of the ones before it. Keep the two files' copies separate as they are -- they share no module state.

review.title: `should not throw on an unparseable regex when no rows are scanned` (index.test.ts:238) is a test that cannot fail under any implementation of the code, guarded or unguarded. It adds maintenance surface and zero coverage.
review.detail:
`should not throw on an unparseable regex when no rows are scanned` (index.test.ts:238) is a test that cannot fail under any implementation of the code, guarded or unguarded. It adds maintenance surface and zero coverage.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.test.ts:238`

Evidence: The block opens a fresh database, runs initSQL, and issues one SELECT against a table with no rows. SQLite only invokes a user function when it scans a row, so `regexp` is never called; the query returns [] whether `regexp` has a try/catch or not. The work order asked for this case explicitly (AC-5's how_to_verify: "The empty-table case is included deliberately to pin the harness behaviour"), but the rationale does not survive contact with the assertion: the query's outcome is decided by the table being empty, not by the guard. Verified with node:sqlite — an UNFIXED `regexp` over an empty table returns [] and does not throw.

Fix: Delete the block. The harness fact it means to pin is already carried by the neighbouring test's comment at line 209-212 ("SQLite only calls a user function when it scans a row"), which sits on a test that does exercise the guard. Alternatively keep it only if it is rewritten to assert something falsifiable.

failure_packet.raw_excerpt:
sdlc: the agent did not write qa-report.json.
It reported success, so it ran — it just put the file somewhere else, or never wrote one.
JSON files that do exist: .nano-staged.json, .oxfmtrc.json, .oxlintrc.json, knip.json, package.json, tsconfig.json, tsconfig.root.json, work-order.json, .sdlc/flow-graph.json, .sdlc/manifest.json
failure_packet.digest: The qa stage failed and no known error pattern matched. The raw output is below.
failure_packet.decision_reason: an agent reads the failed run's full log and decides what happens next — this script cannot see that log from inside the run that produced it

triage.diagnosis: The QA agent ran to completion and did its job; it just never wrote the one file the workflow gates on. The action returned subtype=success, is_error=false after 323 turns / 51 minutes / $20.19, so the step is green, and the agent left 24 evidence files in qa-evidence/ (a 636-line three-file Playwright suite, 19 screenshots, a HAR, a trace, plus an out-of-band better-sqlite3 check against the Electron registration). check-evidence.mjs then said the report could not be read and the judge's validate rejected it by name — but that is the last step of a long chain, not the break. The break is that nothing in the qa workflow looks at what the agent actually did. The action writes the full transcript to _temp/claude-execution-output.json and the log prints only a metadata line about it; sdlc-qa.yml gives the agent step no id, never runs jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq over that file, and never calls agent-transcript.mjs --recover. sdlc-plan.yml and sdlc-root-cause.yml both do all three, and agent-transcript.mjs was written for exactly this failure (growth-os #20: an agent that reported success and wrote neither expected file). QA is the one agent-emitting stage with no transcript recovery, so this failure mode is structurally invisible here: whether the Write was refused, was aimed at a path outside the upload list, or was simply never made is not answerable from anything this run kept. A prior instance is recorded in the workflow's own comment at sdlc-qa.yml:620-622 ('validate then said the agent did not write qa-report.json and triage answered with another browser session'), and the fix applied then tightened the artifact download — which was a different failure and is why this one recurred undiagnosed. I did not rule out a bad agent run, and I am not claiming one: the evidence shows the suite was built and run and the fix's guard verified working on both platforms, so the QA work is sound. What is missing is not the testing, it is the report and any way to see why it was not written. That is a defect in the pipeline's plumbing, so it escalates rather than re-running: a rerun would burn another ~$20 and ~50 minutes to reach the same dead end, and the next agent would have exactly as much visibility as this one did.
triage.evidence: test job, 'Test it, adversarially': {"type":"result","subtype":"success","is_error":false,"duration_ms":3098783,"num_turns":323,"total_cost_usd":20.19} — success, then 'Did the evidence survive?' logs 'the QA report cannot be read (ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'qa-report.json')', and judge logs 'sdlc: the agent did not write qa-report.json'. Meanwhile upload-artifact reports 'there will be 24 files uploaded' and the qa-evidence artifact (ID 11218775655, 16569296 bytes) downloads intact in judge — so the evidence survived and only the report is missing. The workflow gap: .github/workflows/sdlc-qa.yml has no `id:` on the agent step (so no `steps.<id>.outputs.execution_file`, cf. sdlc-plan.yml:360 and sdlc-root-cause.yml:333), no `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq` step, and no `agent-transcript.mjs` call (grep for 'transcript' in sdlc-qa.yml returns nothing), while agent-transcript.mjs's own header names this exact failure ('ran 22 turns, reported success, and wrote neither work-order.json nor stop.json ... triage could not tell a Write that was refused from one never made'). Survived work, if a person wants it: PR #11 (OPEN, MERGEABLE, head b635e0f), artifact qa-evidence with qa-evidence/spec/{regexp,regexp-edge}.spec.ts + fixtures.ts, electron-variant-check.txt showing the guard returning 0 for `\`, `#\`, `#[`, `(` and 1 for `#mortgage` on better-sqlite3, and served-tree-probe.txt confirming the preview serves _pr/ at b635e0f with the guard present. Ruled out: transient/outage/limit (a 51-minute agent run completed with is_error=false, no 429/529/timeout, and prior_signatures is empty); a defect in the app's own code (served-tree-probe and electron-variant-check both show the PR's guard installed and semantically correct); a bad work order (work-order.json is intact on the ledger at version 1 and QA's suite maps to its six acceptance criteria).

framework_defect.what: The QA agent step carries no id, no step runs `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq` over the action's execution file, and no step calls `.sdlc/bin/agent-transcript.mjs --recover qa-report.json` — so when the QA agent finishes without writing qa-report.json, nothing records whether the Write was refused, went to a path outside the upload list, or was never made. sdlc-plan.yml and sdlc-root-cause.yml both wire all three, and agent-transcript.mjs exists for precisely this case; QA is the one artifact-emitting stage with no transcript recovery, which is why run 36983695548 produced only 'the agent did not write qa-report.json' and dispatch-fix classified it error_type=unknown. Its SHAPES map also has no 'qa-report.json' entry, so --recover would need one (keys: verdict, issue, attempt, tests, acceptance_rollup, next_action).
framework_defect.fix: Give the QA agent step an id (e.g. `id: qa_agent`), add a step after it — `if: always()`, env EXEC from `steps.qa_agent.outputs.execution_file` — running `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq "$EXEC" > qa-transcript.json || true`, add qa-transcript.json to the qa-evidence upload path list, and add a `--recover qa-report.json` invocation of agent-transcript.mjs in the judge job before the validate step; extend SHAPES in .sdlc/bin/agent-transcript.mjs with the qa-report.json key list. That makes a recovered report subject to the same validator and gates as a written one, and prints the tool-call metadata that lets triage tell a refused Write from a missing one.
